Acceptance summary:

How fluid flow and cilia motility modulate robust and reproducible patterning events in the embryo is of great interest to a large audience of scientists, both in developmental biology and more disease oriented disciplines. Cilia motility controls the embryonic cerebrospinal fluid circulating between the brain ventricles and the central canal in the spinal cord, failure of which could lead to congenital disease. This work studying cerebrospinal fluid dynamics in the living zebrafish embryo, exploiting imaging, genetics and modelling approaches, sheds new light on a particular mechanical integration between cilia motility and fluid movements within the cerebrospinal canal. Of particular interest is that deficiency in fluid movement can impairs robust morphogenesis and embryonic growth, raising the possibility that similar defects may compromise similar events in human. The precise effectors of cilia motility and the anatomy of the systems of canal where fluids flow will require future work. This study will certainly stimulate others in the field to build on the authors’ working model.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Origin of bidirectionality of cerebrospinal fluid flow and impact on long range transport between brain and spinal cord" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Didier Stainier as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Andrej Vilfan (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This is a highly interesting study of fluid flow in the central canal. The paper first presents in vivo maps of the cilia and the flow, then provides a simple model for the bidirectional velocity distribution, showing that the cilia-induced pressure difference helps maintaining the shape of the canal and discussing the implications of the bi-directional flow for particle transport (which has the properties of enhanced diffusion) and embryogenesis. The study describes an automated workflow of bidirectional CSF flow assessment in the central canal (CC) of the zebrafish spinal cord as well as of CC geometry and cilia localization, which the authors can closely mimic in their modeling attempts. Mutant lines with defects in ciliary motility are analyzed using this workflow, demonstrating a reduced CC diameter (a collapse) in mutants. The manuscript concludes with the description of a novel, so-far overlooked, anatomical feature of the zebrafish central nervous system (Figure 7): while the central canal should run all the way from the ventral diencephalon to the caudal end of the spinal cord and is connected to the diencephalon by a newly discovered funnel cranially, the rhombencephalon extends a novel, much thinner canal dorsally which connects to the CC caudally by another thin canal. If this claim can be substantiated, this finding definitely warrants publication in eLife.

Essential revisions:

1) The existence of the newly described channel, that – if true – needs to be named, has to be proven beyond reasonable doubt, which requires in depth histology, ideally at TEM resolution. The brain anatomy in Figure 7A and Video 8 are not clear, particularly the identity and connection of brain ventricles to CC and the new canal, which is actually not displayed except as a thin line in the scheme in Figure 7A. In other vertebrates (amphibians through mammals), the diencephalon harbors a blind-ending ventral protrusion of the ventricle, which will give rise to the neural part of the hypophysis. Do we see flow in the hypophysis protrusion of the diencephalon in Video 8? Would the hypophysis then be connected to the CC? Why should the rhombencephalon not be connected to the CC, which is what we know from all other vertebrates? This might be an ancestral feature of basal vertebrates, which would be extremely interesting in an evolutionary context, but it needs to be proven. Known canal-like connections in vertebrate embryos include the buccohypophyseal (ventral diencephalon) and neurenteric canals (caudal neural tube/spinal cord). How do the described canals relate to the new one?

2) It is very interesting to see that in ciliary motility mutants the CC collapses and CC flow is abolished. The authors speculate about potential function of CC flow and exosomes transported along the CC. Based on the mutant phenotypes, what specific function of CC flow can be derived? One would really like to learn more about the physiological function of CC flow. A careful analysis/discussion of spinal cord phenotypes in mutants should provide the/an answer.

3) The authors argue that 30 hpf is the ideal time point for their analysis. With the improved automated workflow at hand, the descriptive part of this work would gain a lot by relating this stage to earlier and later time points, particularly with respect to the novel canal.

4) Is it possible to know more about the few motile dorsal cilia: how many are they? Are they polarized, i.e. would they contribute to bi-directional flow? Where are they found along the cranial-caudal axis?

5) Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1:

The zig-zag pattern of some cilia in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A illustrates some challenges when inferring the ciliary beating frequency from a single pixel intensity, which is a highly non-linear function of the cilium's phase. In the middle of the zig-zag line, the principal peak in the power spectrum will likely correspond to the second harmonic of the beating frequency. Aliasing can be an additional problem (the 2nd harmonic of a cilium beating with 40 Hz appears at 20 Hz when sampled with 100 fps). The description in Materials and methods is unclear on how these problems were dealt with.

6) Equation (4): the force density fvchanged its sign between Equations (2) and (4).

7) Equation (5): The zero flux condition (5) must have been taken into account in the derivation of Equations (3) and (4), which always give v=0 at y=d/2. Yet it is only introduced afterwards.

In the subsequent text, the value of α is given, but not that of the viscosity mu. The pressure gradient, which is half the value of fv, is presented as a numerical result, rather than a basic symmetry property of the model.

8) "Counterintuitively, this model predicts that vortices may originate not from cilia dynamics, but rather from the local absence of motile cilia in the ventral side on a distance larger than d."

What is the basis for this statement? What is meant by "cilia dynamics"? It is clear that cilia and gaps between them are both needed to get recirculation.

Moreover, the solution shows an interesting mirror symmetry about the center of the channel, which is not discussed. But it is easy to understand, considering that the velocity profile remains unchanged if any force profile f(y,z)=f(z) (i.e., independent of y) is added to the channel. The force distribution in Figure 3 can therefore always be made antisymmetric with respect to the channel center.

9) Figure 7: the funnel and the loop through RV are very difficult to see – it would be helpful to redesign the figure and make a magnification of the relevant region.

The key point is to solve the general issue of the presumed canal system, especially given its transient nature. Some guidelines are provided below to address this issue.

Reviewer #2:

I like to repeat myself and state again that this manuscript by Wyart, Gallaire and colleagues is mainly technical and descriptive in nature (it lacks a hypothesis). It describes a novel, transient canal system in the embryonic zebrafish CNS; an automated workflow of bidirectional CSF flow assessment in the central canal (CC) of the zebrafish spinal cord as well as of CC geometry and cilia localization, which the authors can closely mimic in their modeling attempts. Several of the features of CC flow described here have been previously reported (by the same authors), though not at the resolution achieved here.

The novelty that qualifies this manuscript for eLife lies primarily in the description of the presumed novel channel system in the embryonic CNS. The revised manuscript contains a limited set of additional histological data that should prove the existence of these canals. Unfortunately, rather than being convinced, I now have doubts as to their existence.

The most parsimonious explanation for these canals would be that they represent aspects of the ventricle in contact with the floor plate ('tel- and diencephalospinal canals') and roof plate ('rhombencephalospinal canal') of the developing brain and spinal cord, with a temporal occlusion in between due to lateral walls getting in close contact (explaining why there is no fluid flow). In the chick embryo, Gary Schoenwolf has studied such a temporal occlusion back in the 1980s already. A wealth of published histological sections in various vertebrate embryos attest that brain ventricle walls as well as lateral walls of the spinal cord approach each other temporarily during development (cf. examples below). The transversal sections shown in the new Figure 7B2 and B4 can be interpreted in exactly that way. Zooming in on the DSC – or perhaps ventricle close to the floor plate – the tear-drop (with flattened bottom) shape of the presumed canal actually argues that this structure is not closed dorsally, which is visible in the ZO-1 stained specimen in B4, in which staining is continuous from the ventral-most aspect (DSC/FP) all along the lateral walls into the wide lumen of the rhombencephalon. The 'similar geometry' of Reissner's fiber and the ventral canal in addition argues that this canal represents the ventral most part of the ventricle next to the floor plate.

Because this issue is of central importance for the main message of this (descriptive) manuscript, it needs to be addressed beyond reasonable doubt: we have to be one hundred percent certain as to the nature of the described items. I think this is feasible without much effort and would include conventional histology, immunofluorescence staining and the analysis of some marker genes. I would suggest to stain WT specimens for mRNA expression of floor and roof plate marker genes (shh, BMP4, etc.) as well as for genes that highlight the dorso-ventral pattering of the brain and neural tube (pax6, nkx2.2 or the like). Stained specimens should be analyzed by conventional histology through transversal sections, such as in Figure 7B4. IF-staining for basal lamina-specific markers should be applied in addition to prove or disprove the existence of these canals.

If it turned out that the canals represented indeed merely the continuation of the ventricle lumen next to floor and roof plate, the manuscript would need to be rewritten. Whether or not it would still qualify for eLife is hard to judge at this point; it would need another round of thorough reviewing.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Origin and role of the cerebrospinal fluid bidirectional flow in the central canal" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Didier Stainier (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below. The critical issues have been adequately addressed and the reviewers believe the work will receive considerable attention in the field. They however identified a few remaining points where simple text revisions will be required before acceptance, as outlined below. Overall, the authors are asked to eliminate the term canal and explain that further work is needed to clarify its geometry.

Reviewer #2:

Nature of the report:

As stated by the authors: we disagree on this point. Although the authors use state-of-the-art technology to visualize and model cilia and CSF flow in the developing zebrafish ventricular system, the main character of the study is descriptive; it lacks a conceptual advance, i.e. it remains unclear what the physiological meaning of bi-directionality is and how the specific pattern of flow relates to any ciliopathies.

Anatomy in question:

Unfortunately, the revised manuscript still lacks clarity. It now seems obvious that the structures the authors report – "conduction paths" (termed "canals" in the former versions of the manuscript, a term that persists in the revised manuscript as well) – represent the dorsal and ventral aspects of the developing ventricular system. This should be clearly stated in the manuscript, not only given as a possible explanation in the Discussion. Canals and conduction paths are confusing and imprecise; in addition, such terms tend to stick, which would be inappropriate. The cited paper by the Sive lab shows a parasagittal section, which does not resolve whether or not these structures are part of the ventricle and provides no proof for the existence of novel conduction paths. In addition, the Ribeiro et al. paper nicely shows that during transition of the neural tube primitive lumen into the central canal, the lumen becomes very narrow, but remains continuous between its dorsal and ventral aspects. If the authors insisted that their conduction paths and canals were independent entities, 3D imaging or morphing of histological sections and segmentation of the ventricular system would be required.

claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from cilia dynamics analysis.

claims.claim: Some cilia beat at lower frequency (~13 Hz) with more complex and irregular patterns.
claims.source: While some cilia beat at high frequency (up to45 Hz, see Materials and methods) with a single frequency pattern, others beat at lower frequency (~13 Hz) with more complex and irregular patterns.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from cilia dynamics analysis.

claims.claim: Motile ventral cilia were four times more numerous than the dorsal ones.
claims.source: Motile ventral cilia were four times more numerous than the dorsal ones.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from quantification of cilia.

claims.claim: Ventral motile cilia were typically 5.8 μm long and beat at 38.1 Hz with a caudal tilt of 62.6° towards the tail.
claims.source: Ventral motile cilia were typically 5.8 μm long and beat at 38.1 Hz with a caudal tilt of 62.6° towards the tail (median of the absolute value, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from quantification of cilia parameters.

claims.claim: Ventral cilia length corresponds to a height of 2.7 μm in the central canal, representing a bit less than half of the central canal on the ventral side.
claims.source: This cilia length corresponds to a height of 2.7 μm in the CC, representing a bit less than half of the CC on the ventral side.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on cilia length measurements.

claims.claim: The beating frequencies measured were higher than the 12–15 Hz previously reported in zebrafish central canal.
claims.source: The beating frequencies we measured were higher than the 12–15 Hz previously reported in zebrafish CC (Kramer-Zucker et al., 2005) (see Materials and methods for a possible explanation), but are consistent with beating frequencies of ependymal cilia located in the brain ventricles of rats (Smith et al., 2012) and zebrafish larvae (Olstad et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison with previous reports, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The measured beating frequencies are consistent with beating frequencies of ependymal cilia located in the brain ventricles of rats and zebrafish larvae.
claims.source: The beating frequencies we measured were higher than the 12–15 Hz previously reported in zebrafish CC (Kramer-Zucker et al., 2005) (see Materials and methods for a possible explanation), but are consistent with beating frequencies of ependymal cilia located in the brain ventricles of rats (Smith et al., 2012) and zebrafish larvae (Olstad et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison with other reports, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Dorsal motile cilia were sparse and evenly distributed along the rostro-caudal axis.
claims.source: Dorsal motile cilia were sparse and evenly distributed along the rostro-caudal axis: they beat with a slightly smaller central frequency (~32 Hz, Figure 2C2), but exhibited similar properties to ventral cilia otherwise (see Figure 2C3, 4, caudal polarization of 59.7 °, length of 5.5 μm).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from quantification of dorsal cilia, with reference to Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Dorsal motile cilia beat with a slightly smaller central frequency (~32 Hz).
claims.source: Dorsal motile cilia were sparse and evenly distributed along the rostro-caudal axis: they beat with a slightly smaller central frequency (~32 Hz, Figure 2C2), but exhibited similar properties to ventral cilia otherwise (see Figure 2C3, 4, caudal polarization of 59.7 °, length of 5.5 μm).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from quantification of dorsal cilia, with reference to Figure 2C2.

claims.claim: Dorsal motile cilia have a caudal polarization of 59.7° and length of 5.5 μm.
claims.source: Dorsal motile cilia were sparse and evenly distributed along the rostro-caudal axis: they beat with a slightly smaller central frequency (~32 Hz, Figure 2C2), but exhibited similar properties to ventral cilia otherwise (see Figure 2C3, 4, caudal polarization of 59.7 °, length of 5.5 μm).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from quantification of dorsal cilia, with reference to Figure 2C3, 4.

claims.claim: Theoretical and numerical predictions are in good agreement with the 57 velocity profiles measured in vivo.
claims.source: Theoretical and numerical predictions are in good agreement with the 57 velocity profiles measured in vivo and tested here (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison between model predictions and experimental data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Numerical simulations show that recirculation regions appear between spots of constant volume force.
claims.source: With this 'sparse cilia' model, numerical simulations show that recirculation regions appear between these spots (Figure 3C2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from numerical simulations, with reference to Figure 3C2.

claims.claim: Differences in beating frequency between active neighboring cilia lead to the emergence of recirculation regions.
claims.source: We can further show that differences in beating frequency between active neighboring cilia lead to the emergence of the same recirculation regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: In all mutants with defective cilia (elipsa, lrrc50, foxj1anw2, kurly), no particles entered the central canal even several hours post injection in anaesthetized mutant embryos.
claims.source: In all these mutants with defective cilia, we injected beads in the DV/MV, but we could not observe the beads transported inside the CC. In anaesthetized mutant embryos, no particles entered the CC even several hours post injection, as illustrated here in elipsa embryos (Figure 4A1 and A2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in mutants, with reference to Figure 4A1 and A2.

claims.claim: Long-range transport of beads down the central canal is altered in mutants with defective cilia.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with previous reports (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018) showing that long-range transport of beads down the central canal is altered in mutants with defective cilia.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with previous reports, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The central canal diameter was dramatically reduced in all mutants tested: elipsa, lrrc50, foxj1anw2, and kurly.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we observed that the CC diameter was dramatically reduced in all mutants tested: elipsa, lrrc50, foxj1anw2, and kurly (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in mutants, with reference to Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: The central canal is flattened along the D-V axis and not as straight as control siblings in mutants with defective cilia.
claims.source: Although the CC forms in these mutants, it is flattened along the D-V axis and not as straight as control siblings (Figure 4B1, B2 and C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in mutants, with reference to Figure 4B1, B2 and C.

claims.claim: For scospondinicm15/icm15 mutants, which are curled down but exhibit normal cilia activity, no difference in the central canal diameter was measured.
claims.source: In order to evaluate whether these features could be due to the convex body curvature of the embryos, we analyzed the CC structure of mutant embryos scospondinicm15/icm15, which are also curled down but exhibit normal cilia activity (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018). For these mutants, we did not measure any difference in the CC diameter.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in scospondin mutants, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Cilia integrity and motility are critical to properly form the central canal and instruct its diameter and straightness.
claims.source: This observation suggests that cilia integrity and motility are critical to properly form the CC and instruct its diameter and straightness.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observations in mutants.

claims.claim: Allowing mutant embryos to spontaneously twitch facilitated the transport of beads down the central canal.
claims.source: However, we noticed that allowing mutant embryos to spontaneously twitch (by not anesthetizing them before imaging) facilitated the transport of beads down the CC (see next section for the characterization of the effect of muscle contraction on CSF flow).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in mutants.

claims.claim: Fluorescent beads in the central canal of elipsa and kurly mostly undergo random Brownian motion, but some allow to measure a residual flow with many recirculation zones.
claims.source: By using the effect of muscle contractions, we were able to get beads down the CC in mutants with a moderate reduction of the CC diameter, such as elipsa and kurly. Fluorescent beads in the CC of elipsa and kurly mostly undergo random Brownian motion, but some allow to measure a residual flow with many recirculation zones (Video 4), in good agreement with the predictions of the sparse cilia model.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in mutants, with reference to Video 4.

claims.claim: The bidirectional CSF flow in the central canal is generated locally and does not rely on a global pressure gradient generated in the ventricles.
claims.source: It is also predicted that the bidirectional CSF flow in the CC is generated locally and does not rely on a global pressure gradient generated in the ventricles.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: Even after large regions without cilia and local flow, the CSF flow in more caudal regions can show a bidirectional flow, as long as motile cilia beat locally in the ventral region.
claims.source: This is confirmed by multiple observations: i) even after large regions without cilia and local flow, the CSF flow in more caudal regions can show a bidirectional flow, as long as motile cilia beat locally in the ventral region (as predicted by Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation confirming the model prediction, with reference to Figure 3C.

claims.claim: When a portion of the central canal of around 200 μm in length is isolated by using photoablation to block flow on both extremities, the canal kept its diameter at the center and the CSF still flowed bidirectionally.
claims.source: ii) When a portion of the CC of around 200 μm in length is isolated by using photoablation to block flow on both extremities (see Materials and methods and Figure 4D1), the canal kept its diameter at the center and the CSF still flowed bidirectionally (Video 5) with a similar velocity profile (Figure 4D2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from photoablation experiments, with reference to Figure 4D1, D2 and Video 5.

claims.claim: Following each muscle contraction, rapid displacements of CSF were observed in either the caudal or rostral direction, followed by a slower counter-flow in the opposite direction.
claims.source: Following each contraction, rapid displacements of CSF (too fast to be properly characterized) were observed in either the caudal or rostral direction, followed by a slower counter-flow in the opposite direction, whose velocity decayed until the original bidirectional flow is recovered (Figure 5B and C, Video 6, Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in contracting embryos, with reference to Figure 5B and C, Video 6, Video 7.

claims.claim: The average CSF flow throughout the entire central canal section is correlated with the instantaneous muscle contractions.
claims.source: The average CSF flow throughout the entire CC section is correlated with the instantaneous muscle contractions (Figure 5D) and showed a sudden increase after contractions.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in contracting embryos, with reference to Figure 5D.

claims.claim: A robust flow rate increase was observed after each contraction.
claims.source: By comparing the increase in CSF flow over 5 s after each contraction with the contraction strength, we observed a robust flow rate increase after each contraction (Figure 5E; 204 contractions from 22 WT embryos).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in contracting embryos, with reference to Figure 5E.

claims.claim: No correlation was found between the flow direction and estimates of the contraction direction or strength.
claims.source: However, we did not find any correlation between the flow direction and estimates of the contraction direction or strength.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in contracting embryos.

claims.claim: Body contractions enhance transport of beads in mutants with defective cilia.
claims.source: Body contractions also enhance transport of beads in mutants with defective cilia, as mentioned in the previous section (Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in mutants, with reference to Video 4.

claims.claim: No significant difference in the central canal diameter was detected during the muscle contractions.
claims.source: As no significant difference in the CC diameter was detected during the muscle contractions, we propose that the reported enhancement of CSF flow is not due to a local variation of the CC diameter, but instead due to a change in the volume of the brain ventricles that occurs during muscle contraction at larval stage (Olstad et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in contracting embryos, with a citation.

claims.claim: The enhancement of CSF flow is due to a change in the volume of the brain ventricles that occurs during muscle contraction at larval stage.
claims.source: As no significant difference in the CC diameter was detected during the muscle contractions, we propose that the reported enhancement of CSF flow is not due to a local variation of the CC diameter, but instead due to a change in the volume of the brain ventricles that occurs during muscle contraction at larval stage (Olstad et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a proposed explanation, with a citation.

claims.claim: CSF long-range transport of nanoparticles has characteristics of both passive diffusion and active transport.
claims.source: Here, we first demonstrate experimentally that CSF long-range transport of nanoparticles has characteristics of both passive diffusion and active transport.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claims.claim: The particle transport follows an apparent diffusive law, as the propagation front of nanoparticles progresses with the square root of time.
claims.source: The particle transport follows an apparent diffusive law, as the propagation front of nanoparticles progresses with the square root of time (Zhang et al., 2018) and this propagation is found to be slower for larger particle size (Figure 6A1 and A2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with a citation and reference to Figure 6A1 and A2.

claims.claim: The propagation of nanoparticles is found to be slower for larger particle size.
claims.source: The particle transport follows an apparent diffusive law, as the propagation front of nanoparticles progresses with the square root of time (Zhang et al., 2018) and this propagation is found to be slower for larger particle size (Figure 6A1 and A2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 6A1 and A2.

claims.claim: The propagation front of 20 nm-diameter fluorescent beads is accelerated by muscle contractions, when the local CSF flow velocity is increased.
claims.source: On the other hand, the propagation front of 20 nm-diameter fluorescent beads is accelerated by muscle contractions, when the local CSF flow velocity is increased (Figure 6A2 and A3).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 6A2 and A3.

claims.claim: 20 nm-diameter fluorescent beads injected in the DV/MV are found to travel through the entire length of central canal (~2 mm) in about two hours.
claims.source: Indeed, 20 nm-diameter fluorescent beads injected in the DV/MV are found to travel through the entire length of CC (~2 mm) in about two hours (Figure 6A2), far from the timescales expected for passive diffusion (over one day) or pure ballistic transport at the speed of the flow (with V = 5 μm/s, this would lead to less than 10 min).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Figure 6A2.

claims.claim: The effective diffusivity is higher in the case of contracting embryos compared to paralyzed embryos.
claims.source: In vivo front tracking experiments illustrate this flow-induced accelerated transport of 20 nm nanoparticles in paralyzed and contracting zebrafish embryos (Figure 6D). While both contracting and paralyzed embryos exhibit a diffusive-like transport, the effective diffusivity is higher in the case of contracting embryos.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Muscle contractions can increase the long-range transport efficiency.
claims.source: It confirms that muscle contractions can increase the long-range transport efficiency (an increase of the steady bidirectional velocity would have similar effects, Figure 6C1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study, with reference to Figure 6C1.

claims.claim: The transport is predicted to be enhanced in both rostro-caudal and caudo-rostral directions.
claims.source: Interestingly, the transport is predicted to be enhanced in both rostro-caudal and caudo-rostral directions, which is confirmed by in vivo experiments.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model confirmed by experiments.

claims.claim: When injected locally in the caudal part of the central canal, fluorescent nanobeads are transported rostrally towards the brain ventricles.
claims.source: When injected locally in the caudal part of the CC, fluorescent nanobeads are indeed transported rostrally towards the brain ventricles (Figure 6E1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Figure 6E1.

claims.claim: The reverse transport is sped up in contracting embryos.
claims.source: Similarly to rostral-to-caudal transport, the reverse transport is sped up incontracting embryos (Figure 6E2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Figure 6E2.

claims.claim: At 30 hpf, cilia in the brain ventricles are mostly non-motile.
claims.source: At this stage, cilia in the brain ventricles are mostly non-motile (Olstad et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact, with a citation.

claims.claim: At 30 hpf, CSF flow in the brain ventricles is mostly Brownian, although the heart beat is responsible for a pulsatile component to the flow at the heart beat frequency.
claims.source: At this stage, CSF flow in the brain ventricles is mostly Brownian, although the heart beat is responsible for a pulsatile component to the flow at the heart beat frequency (Video 8), as previously observed (Fame et al., 2016; Olstad et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with citations and reference to Video 8.

claims.claim: Before 30 hpf CSF flow in the brain ventricles does not contribute to the overall CSF circulation.
claims.source: Our observations indicate that before 30 hpf CSF flow in the brain ventricles does not contribute to the overall CSF circulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observations.

claims.claim: The diameter of the ventral opening of the RV primitive lumen is smaller than the central canal diameter (7.1 ± 0.7 μm) and is 233 ± 24 μm long.
claims.source: We measured that the diameter of this ventral opening is smaller than the CC diameter (7.1 ± 0.7 μm) and is 233 ± 24 μm long (Figure 7A and B – green arrow, 7C,11 embryos, Video 9) and that few motile cilia enable there a unidirectional flow from rostral to caudal, that is towards the CC (Video 10).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from measurements in 11 embryos, with reference to Figure 7A, B, C and Video 9, 10.

claims.claim: Few motile cilia enable a unidirectional flow from rostral to caudal in the ventral opening of the RV primitive lumen.
claims.source: We measured that the diameter of this ventral opening is smaller than the CC diameter (7.1 ± 0.7 μm) and is 233 ± 24 μm long (Figure 7A and B – green arrow, 7C,11 embryos, Video 9) and that few motile cilia enable there a unidirectional flow from rostral to caudal, that is towards the CC (Video 10).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Video 10.

claims.claim: This fast and unidirectional flow follows a parabolic Poiseuille-like velocity profile with a maximum speed of 15 μm / s.
claims.source: This fast and unidirectional flow follows a parabolic Poiseuille-like velocity profile with a maximum speed of 15 μm / s (Figure 7D1 and D2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Figure 7D1 and D2.

claims.claim: The central canal primitive lumen is composed of two main openings, with a very narrow but continuous connection between the two.
claims.source: The CC pL is indeed composed of two main openings, with a very narrow but continuous connection between the two (Kondrychyn et al., 2013, Ribeiro et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact, with citations.

claims.claim: The apical domains of the two openings of the central canal primitive lumen, marked with the tight junctions protein ZO-1, are closely-spaced, so that CSF flow is independent in each opening.
claims.source: We observed that the apical domains of the two openings of the CC pL, marked with the tight junctions protein ZO-1, are closely-spaced, so that CSF flow is independent in each opening (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The central canal ventral and dorsal openings converge into a single opening, dense in motile cilia, in the caudal part of the spinal cord.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the CC ventral and dorsal openings converge into a single opening, dense in motile cilia, in the caudal part of the spinal cord (Figure 7 E2, Video 12).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Figure 7 E2 and Video 12.

claims.claim: During development, dorsal and ventral openings of the central canal primitive lumen converge ventrally at three dpf.
claims.source: During development, as it has already been partly described in rodents and zebrafish (Sevc et al., 2009; Kondrychyn et al., 2013, Ribeiro et al., 2017), dorsal and ventral openings of the CC pL converge ventrally at three dpf (Figure 7F) to finally merge into a single central canal lumen at five dpf (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with citations and reference to Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Dorsal and ventral openings of the central canal primitive lumen finally merge into a single central canal lumen at five dpf.
claims.source: During development, as it has already been partly described in rodents and zebrafish (Sevc et al., 2009; Kondrychyn et al., 2013, Ribeiro et al., 2017), dorsal and ventral openings of the CC pL converge ventrally at three dpf (Figure 7F) to finally merge into a single central canal lumen at five dpf (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with citations and reference to Figure 7G.

claims.claim: Half of the ablated larvae were shorter in length than siblings that underwent a control ablation of the yolk extension or had no ablation, 30 hr after ablation at the beginning of the central canal.
claims.source: We performed 2-photon mediated photo-ablations at the beginning of the CC to disconnect the CC from the brain ventricles (Figure 8A1 and A2). We found that 30 hr after ablation, half of the ablated larvae were shorter in length than siblings that underwent a control ablation of the yolk extension or had no ablation (Figure 8B1 and B2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from ablation experiments, with reference to Figure 8A1, A2, B1 and B2.

claims.claim: Larvae with the opening ablated had an increase in body-axis curvature.
claims.source: Larvae with the opening ablated had an increase in body-axis curvature (Figure 8C1 and C2).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from ablation experiments, with reference to Figure 8C1 and C2.

claims.claim: Global CSF circulation contributes to embryonic growth.
claims.source: These experiments indicate that global CSF circulation contributes to embryonic growth, and suggest that the transport of particles between brain and spinal cord is a critical process for development.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ablation experiments.

claims.claim: The transport of particles between brain and spinal cord is a critical process for development.
claims.source: These experiments indicate that global CSF circulation contributes to embryonic growth, and suggest that the transport of particles between brain and spinal cord is a critical process for development.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ablation experiments.

claims.claim: Full field optical coherence tomography imaging of 30 hpf embryos reveals high density of secreted vesicles in central canal.
claims.source: In order to find particles that could be efficiently transported by the bidirectional flow, we investigated the content of the CSF and identified abundant extracellular vesicles using the label-free imaging technique, full field optical coherence tomography (Figure 8D and Video 13).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Figure 8D and Video 13.

claims.claim: Numerous vesicles with high lipids or proteins content filled the central canal.
claims.source: Numerous vesicles with high lipids or proteins content filled the CC, in agreement with previous observations (Sternberg et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with a citation.

claims.claim: Some of the particles in the CSF may correspond to exosomes.
claims.source: Fluorescent labeling of CD63 (Video 14, Materials and methods) and electron microscopy with immunogold labeling of exosomes suggested that some of these particles may correspond to exosomes in the CSF (Figure 8E, Materials and methods) (Verweij et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with a citation and reference to Figure 8E and Video 14.

claims.claim: Electron microscopy reveals a variety of other extracellular vesicles, such as lipoparticles, microvesicles.
claims.source: Electron microscopy also reveals a variety of other extracellular vesicles, such as lipoparticles, microvesicles.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from electron microscopy.

claims.claim: The diameter of these vesicles ranges between 50 and 250 nm.
claims.source: The diameter of these vesicles ranges between 50 and 250 nm (Figure 8E), typically in a regime where Taylor-Aris dispersion is important.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from electron microscopy, with reference to Figure 8E.

claims.claim: The bidirectional flow of endogenous extracellular vesicles can be put in evidence in the central canal using full field optical coherence tomography as well as fluorescence live imaging.
claims.source: The bidirectional flow of endogenous extracellular vesicles can be put in evidence in the CC using full field optical coherence tomography as well as fluorescence live imaging (Video 13, Video 14).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, with reference to Video 13 and Video 14.

claims.claim: The effective CSF circulation contributes to embryonic growth via the transport of extracellular vesicles between brain and spinal cord.
claims.source: Altogether, our works suggests that the effective CSF circulation contributes to embryonic growth via the transport of extracellular vesicles between brain and spinal cord.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: A steady bidirectional CSF flow is driven by ventral motile cilia.
claims.source: In this study, we performed quantification of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation in zebrafish embryos. By combining experiments and modeling, we demonstrated that a steady bidirectional CSF flow is driven by ventral motile cilia and that body movements create additional transient flows.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Body movements create additional transient flows.
claims.source: In this study, we performed quantification of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation in zebrafish embryos. By combining experiments and modeling, we demonstrated that a steady bidirectional CSF flow is driven by ventral motile cilia and that body movements create additional transient flows.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: These two driving forces (cilia and body movements) accelerate the long-range transport of all particles larger than 10 nm, including the many macromolecules and extracellular vesicles present in the central canal.
claims.source: These two driving forces accelerate the long-range transport of all particles larger than 10 nm, including the many macromolecules and extracellular vesicles present in the CC.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Fast transport both from brain to spinal cord, and from spinal cord to the brain, is critical for normal embryonic development.
claims.source: This permits fast transport both from brain to spinal cord, and from spinal cord to the brain, which is critical for normal embryonic development.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: The study focused on embryogenesis as this is a critical period when CSF is most concentrated in secreted extracellular lipid vesicles.
claims.source: Our study focused on embryogenesis as this is a critical period when CSF is most concentrated in secreted extracellular lipid vesicles (Bachy et al., 2008; Tietje et al., 2014), and when blood flow along the body is not established to transport key molecules.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study focus, with citations.

claims.claim: During embryogenesis, blood flow along the body is not established to transport key molecules.
claims.source: Our study focused on embryogenesis as this is a critical period when CSF is most concentrated in secreted extracellular lipid vesicles (Bachy et al., 2008; Tietje et al., 2014), and when blood flow along the body is not established to transport key molecules.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study focus.

claims.claim: The work predicts the establishment of a positive pressure in the central canal, increasing linearly towards the caudal direction.
claims.source: Our work predicts the establishment of a positive pressure in the CC, increasing linearly towards the caudal direction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: This inner pressure is decreased as the density of motile cilia is lower.
claims.source: This inner pressure is decreased as the density of motile cilia is lower.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: Among other roles related to transport of chemical cues or mechano-sensing, the cilia motility ensures the integrity of the central canal, which is necessary for proper body axis formation.
claims.source: This suggests that, among other roles related to transport of chemical cues or mechano-sensing, the cilia motility ensures the integrity of the CC, which is necessary for proper body axis formation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the findings.

claims.claim: Small veins have been reported to collapse under a decrease of inner pressure.
claims.source: Interestingly, small veins have also been reported to collapse under a decrease of inner pressure (Fung, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison, with a citation.

claims.claim: During some fixation processes, if the structure is not maintained fast enough, the loss of cilia activity should lead to a decrease of the inner pressure and to the collapse of the central canal.
claims.source: During some fixation processes, if the structure is not maintained fast enough, the loss of cilia activity should lead to a decrease of the inner pressure and to the collapse of the CC.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculation about fixation processes.

claims.claim: Mutants with defective cilia were unable to maintain an open central canal.
claims.source: We report that mutants with defective cilia were unable to maintain an open CC.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claims.claim: Elipsa and kurly embryos with partial loss of cilia motility show intermediate phenotypes, with some regions open and other constrained, and with open regions showing bidirectional flow with a higher density of recirculation zones.
claims.source: Elipsa and kurly embryos with partial loss of cilia motility show intermediate phenotypes, with some regions open and other constrained, and with open regions showing bidirectional flow with a higher density of recirculation zones.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claims.claim: These flow patterns are predicted by the sparse cilia model.
claims.source: These flow patterns are predicted by the sparse cilia model (Figure 3C), since a few cilia remain motile in kurly embryos (Jaffe et al., 2016) and in elipsa between 24 hpf and 30 hpf (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison between model predictions and observations, with citations and reference to Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The sparse cilia model accounts for the reduced long-range transport previously observed in kif3b mutants, where cilia density is reduced.
claims.source: It also accounts for the reduced long-range transport previously observed in kif3b mutants, where cilia density is reduced (Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an explanation for previous observations, with a citation.

claims.claim: Foxj1a mutant embryos showing ependymal cells with defective cilia have an almost closed central canal.
claims.source: In contrast, foxj1a mutant embryos showing ependymal cells with defective cilia (Yu et al., 2008) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) have an almost closed CC.

results.result: The CSF flow in the central canal of 30 hpf zebrafish embryos is bidirectional with a characteristic bimodal velocity profile. The flow is positive (rostral to caudal) ventrally with maximal speed of 4.78 ± 0.79 μm/s and negative (caudal to rostral) dorsally with minimal speed of -4.80 ± 0.82 μm/s, reversing at relative D-V position 0.53. The average flow rate through a cross-section is null.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C30 provide detailed quantitative measurements from 110 WT embryos showing the bidirectional nature of the flow with specific velocity values and positions. The symmetry of the profile and null average flow rate are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes and statistical measures (mean ± s.d.). The automated kymograph analysis method is described in detail in Materials and Methods.

results.result: The bidirectional CSF flow is generated locally by caudally-polarized motile cilia along the ventral wall of the central canal. Ventral motile cilia (4x more numerous than dorsal) are typically 5.8 μm long, beat at 38.1 Hz with a 62.6° caudal tilt, occupying about half the canal height (2.7 μm). A theoretical model based on these parameters accurately predicts the observed velocity profiles in 57 embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C43 provide comprehensive quantitative characterization of cilia properties from 89 embryos (1704 motile cilia analyzed). The theoretical model (C3, C47) incorporating these measured parameters successfully predicts experimental velocity profiles, providing strong convergent evidence. The refutation of a global pressure gradient (C31) is logically sound based on the null average flow rate.

results.result: The closed geometry of the central canal imposes a null average flow rate, explaining the bidirectionality. The flow is generated locally and does not rely on a global pressure gradient from the ventricles, as demonstrated by photoablation experiments isolating canal segments that maintain bidirectional flow.
results.evaluation: The geometric constraint explanation (C4) is supported by both theoretical modeling and experimental evidence. The photoablation experiments (C62) provide direct experimental validation that isolated ~200 μm canal segments maintain bidirectional flow with similar velocity profiles, confirming local generation. The observation that caudal regions can show bidirectional flow even after regions without cilia (C61) further supports this conclusion.

results.result: Motile cilia are required for proper formation of the central canal. In mutants with defective cilia (elipsa, lrrc50, foxj1a, kurly), the canal diameter is dramatically reduced and flattened along the D-V axis, while scospondin mutants with normal cilia activity show no diameter reduction. The motile cilia maintaining canal geometry originate from ependymal cells specifically.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 report consistent observations across multiple independent mutant lines affecting different aspects of cilia function. The control experiment with scospondin mutants (C56) that are curled but have normal cilia activity shows no canal diameter reduction, establishing that the effect is specific to cilia function rather than body curvature. The foxj1a mutant analysis (C117-C118) provides additional specificity by showing ependymal cells are the critical source.

results.result: A 'sparse cilia' model predicts that spatial heterogeneity in cilia distribution creates recirculation regions between active ciliated areas. This is confirmed by observations in elipsa and kurly mutants showing residual flow with many recirculation zones, consistent with their partial loss of cilia motility.
results.evaluation: The numerical simulations (C48, C51) make specific predictions about recirculation patterns that are confirmed by experimental observations in mutants with partial cilia loss (C59, C114, C115). The model successfully accounts for previously reported reduced transport in kif3b mutants (C116), providing additional validation across independent datasets.

results.result: Muscle contractions transiently enhance bidirectional CSF flow in the central canal. Following each contraction, rapid CSF displacements occur followed by slower counter-flow, with robust flow rate increases observed after 204 contractions from 22 embryos. The enhancement is likely due to changes in brain ventricle volume rather than local canal diameter changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 provide detailed temporal characterization of flow changes associated with contractions, with substantial sample size (204 contractions, 22 embryos). The lack of correlation between flow direction and contraction direction/strength (C66) is appropriately noted. The proposed mechanism (C69) is reasonable given the citation to similar observations in larvae and the lack of canal diameter changes (C68), though this remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: The bidirectional flow accelerates particle transport in the CSF via a coupled convective-diffusive process (Taylor-Aris dispersion). Transport follows an apparent diffusive law but is faster than pure diffusion and slower than ballistic transport. Muscle contractions further accelerate transport, and enhancement occurs in both rostro-caudal and caudo-rostral directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C79 provide comprehensive experimental evidence (particle tracking in paralyzed vs. contracting embryos) supported by theoretical modeling of Taylor-Aris dispersion. The bidirectional enhancement (C77-C79) is demonstrated experimentally with caudal injections showing rostral transport. The timescale arguments (C74) and size-dependence observations (C72) are consistent with the proposed mechanism. The theoretical derivation in Appendix 2 provides mathematical rigor.

results.result: CSF flows unidirectionally from the diencephalic/mesencephalic ventricle to the central canal entrance. Two-photon ablation of this connection leads to reduced embryo size and increased body-axis curvature 30 hr post-ablation, indicating that global CSF circulation and particle transport between brain and spinal cord are critical for embryonic growth and development.
results.evaluation: The ablation experiments (C91-C92) provide direct functional evidence with appropriate controls (yolk extension ablation, no ablation). The phenotypic effects on length and curvature are statistically significant (p-values provided in Figure 8). However, the mechanistic link to particle transport (C94) remains somewhat inferential, though supported by the broader context of the study including vesicle observations.

results.result: Cilia activity combined with muscle contractions sustains long-range transport of extracellular lipidic particles (50-250 nm diameter), including exosomes and other vesicles, enabling embryonic growth. These vesicles are abundant in the CSF and undergo bidirectional flow, with transport accelerated for all particles larger than 10 nm.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 provide multiple lines of evidence for vesicle presence and transport: FF-OCT imaging, electron microscopy with immunogold labeling, and fluorescent CD63 labeling. The size range (C99) is appropriate for Taylor-Aris dispersion effects. The connection to embryonic growth (C101, C105) is supported by the ablation experiments showing growth defects when circulation is disrupted, though the specific molecular cargo remains to be fully characterized.

results.result: At 30 hpf, a specific CSF circulation is established between brain ventricles and the central canal through transient primitive lumen openings. The ventral opening of the RV primitive lumen (7.1 ± 0.7 μm diameter, 233 ± 24 μm long) has unidirectional flow toward the central canal. The dorsal and ventral openings of the central canal primitive lumen converge at 3 dpf and merge into a single lumen at 5 dpf.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C90 provide detailed anatomical characterization with quantitative measurements from 11 embryos. The developmental progression is documented with imaging at multiple time points (30 hpf, 3 dpf, 5 dpf) and is consistent with previous reports (citations provided). The functional importance (C120) is supported by the ablation experiments. The observation that brain ventricle flow is mostly Brownian at this stage (C81-C82) appropriately distinguishes the developmental timing.

results.result: In anesthetized mutants with defective cilia (elipsa, lrrc50, foxj1a, kurly), no particles enter the central canal even hours post-injection, consistent with altered long-range transport. However, allowing mutant embryos to spontaneously twitch facilitates bead transport down the canal.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 document consistent observations across multiple mutant lines and are consistent with previous reports (citations provided). The rescue by muscle contractions (C58) is an important observation that connects to the role of contractions in enhancing flow. However, the inability to measure local flow in anesthetized mutants limits direct characterization of the flow defects.

results.result: The model predicts establishment of positive pressure in the central canal increasing linearly toward the caudal direction, which decreases with lower cilia density. This pressure maintains canal integrity, necessary for proper body axis formation. The model draws analogy to small vein collapse under decreased inner pressure.
results.evaluation: The pressure predictions (C108-C109) follow logically from the theoretical model and are illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A. The connection to canal integrity (C110) is supported by the mutant phenotypes showing reduced diameter. However, the fixation artifact speculation (C112) and the vein analogy (C111) are more tentative. The overall reasoning is sound but some aspects remain to be directly validated.

results.result: The hydrodynamic model uses a single fitting parameter (α = 0.5) corresponding to a force of 10 pN per cilium, consistent with literature values. The model is robust to force profile variations and can predict flow profiles for various aspect ratios and ciliary beating frequencies, including flows in artificial magnetic cilia microchannels.
results.evaluation: The model validation (C125) shows good agreement with literature values (Hill et al., 2010). The robustness tests (C126) and versatility demonstrations (C127-C128) strengthen confidence in the modeling approach. The successful prediction of Shields et al. (2010) data provides independent validation. The model's simplifications are acknowledged and justified.

results.result: The model neglects dorsal cilia contribution (representing ~20% of motile cilia) because dorsal cilia, also oriented caudally, tend to cancel ventral cilia contributions locally and can create recirculation regions. The bidirectional flow is affected by at most 20% due to sparse dorsal cilia.
results.evaluation: The justification for neglecting dorsal cilia (C129-C132) is reasonable given their sparse distribution and opposing geometric position. The 20% estimate provides an upper bound on the error. The linearity of Stokes equations supports the superposition argument. However, this remains a modeling approximation that could be tested more rigorously.

results.result: The Reissner fiber (RF) was neglected in the model because it does not compartmentalize fluid in 3D and should not qualitatively modify flow bidirectionality, confirmed by velocity profiles in scospondin mutants lacking RF. However, RF absence may alter CSF-contacting neuron activity due to changed mechanical forces. The working model proposes that lack of motile cilia reduces canal diameter, altering RF polymerization and URP peptide expression.
results.evaluation: The justification for neglecting the RF (C133-C135) is supported by experimental data from scospondin mutants. The speculation about neuron activity changes (C136) is appropriately cautious. The working model (C137-C138) integrates multiple observations but remains somewhat speculative regarding the mechanistic sequence. The acknowledgment that why RF fails to form in smaller canals remains unknown is appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: CSF circulation contributes to body axis formation and brain development. The study focused on embryogenesis when CSF is concentrated in extracellular lipid vesicles and blood flow is not established for transport. Various biological flows use different mechanisms: blood flow uses heart-driven pressure gradients, intestinal/lymph flows use peristalsis, and cilia-driven flows are critical for left/right asymmetry and CSF circulation.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C8-C13) provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. The rationale for focusing on embryogenesis (C106-C107) is well-justified. These are primarily contextual claims that frame the study rather than novel findings, but they are accurately stated and properly referenced.

results.result: Previous work by the authors showed bidirectional CSF flow in 24-30 hpf zebrafish embryos. Body-axis defects in cilia mutants appear by 30 hpf, before brain ventricle cilia become motile, suggesting that proper CSF flow dynamics in the central canal rather than brain ventricles is critical for embryonic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 accurately cite previous work including the authors' own studies and others. The inference about central canal importance (C16) is logical based on the temporal sequence, though it remains somewhat indirect. This provides important context and motivation for the current study.

results.result: The study demonstrates that steady bidirectional CSF flow is driven by ventral motile cilia and body movements create additional transient flows. Zebrafish transparency enables characterization of CSF flow and cilia dynamics in the central canal, which is challenging in other species but well-conserved among vertebrates. Findings are expected to guide future mammalian investigations and may impact understanding of development, inflammatory response, and motor circuit functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 accurately summarize the main findings. The rationale for using zebrafish (C139-C140) is sound. The expectations about future impact (C141-C143) are appropriately framed as speculation. These are summary and forward-looking statements that are reasonable given the presented evidence.

results.result: The transient architecture and circulation within primitive lumens may be specific to teleost species where neural tube formation occurs by tissue internalization and cavitation, unlike amniotes where it occurs by tissue folding and fusion. However, evidence exists for similar ventricular wall appositions in amniotes.
results.evaluation: The comparative developmental biology claims (C121-C123) are appropriately cautious and supported by citations. The acknowledgment of potential similarities across species despite different developmental mechanisms is scientifically sound. This represents appropriate contextualization of the findings within broader vertebrate biology.
